post.caption: Galalith jewelry is made from milk. The name comes from Greek words for milk and stone. It is a plastic made from casein, the main protein in milk. Sheets an inch thick soaked in formaldehyde for up to a year. In the 1890s, Wilhelm Krische sought a wipe clean replacement for slate. It failed as a board yet proved useful for many other things. Makers colored it to look like ivory or horn. It could not be molded, so makers cut and carved it. Costume jewelry designers loved it in the 1920s and 1930s. Unlike celluloid, it was virtually nonflammable. Galalith is still made today, mostly for buttons.
